solution:
A conjugate acid-base pair is a pair of species that differ by ONE proton: removing \(\text{H}^+\) from a Brönsted acid gives its conjugate base, and adding \(\text{H}^+\) to a Brönsted base gives its conjugate acid.

Taking each species in the sense in which it normally acts:

\(\text{HNO}_2\) (acid) — conjugate base \(\text{NO}_2^-\)

\(\text{CN}^-\) (base) — conjugate acid \(\text{HCN}\)

\(\text{HClO}_4\) (acid) — conjugate base \(\text{ClO}_4^-\)

\(\text{F}^-\) (base) — conjugate acid \(\text{HF}\)

\(\text{OH}^-\) (base) — conjugate acid \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) (it can also act as an acid, giving the conjugate base \(\text{O}^{2-}\))

\(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) (base) — conjugate acid \(\text{HCO}_3^-\)

\(\text{S}^{2-}\) (base) — conjugate acid \(\text{HS}^-\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the key lists \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) as a Lewis acid alongside \(\text{BF}_3\) and \(\text{H}^{+}\). A Lewis acid must ACCEPT an electron pair, which requires either an incomplete octet or a vacant low-energy orbital. In \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) the nitrogen already has a complete octet with all four pairs used in bonding, no lone pair left over and no vacant valence orbital, so it can neither donate nor accept a pair. The chapter's own \(\S 6.10.3\) illustrates Lewis acids with ELECTRON-DEFICIENT species, which is exactly what \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) is not. Worth knowing why the error is tempting: \(\text{NH}_4^{+}\) IS a BRONSTED acid, since it can give up a proton — but that is a different definition, and under the Lewis definition the species that accepts the electron pair is the \(\text{H}^{+}\) released, not the ammonium ion itself.] A Lewis acid is a species that can ACCEPT a lone pair of electrons, which requires a vacant orbital or an incomplete octet.

\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\): oxygen carries two lone pairs and donates them, so it is a Lewis BASE, not an acid.

\(\text{BF}_3\): boron has only six electrons around it and a vacant \(2p\) orbital, so it accepts a lone pair — a Lewis ACID.

\(\text{H}^+\): a bare proton with an empty \(1s\) orbital, so it accepts a lone pair — a Lewis ACID.

\(\text{NH}_4^+\): nitrogen already has a complete octet with all four pairs used in bonding and no lone pair left, and it has no vacant low-energy orbital, so it can neither donate nor accept an electron pair.

The Lewis acids are \(\text{BF}_3\) and \(\text{H}^+\).

The conjugate base of a Brönsted acid is what remains after the acid donates one proton, so it carries one \(\text{H}\) fewer and one unit more negative charge.

\(\text{HF} \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{F}^-\): conjugate base \(\text{F}^-\)

\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{HSO}_4^-\): conjugate base \(\text{HSO}_4^-\)

\(\text{HCO}_3^- \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{CO}_3^{2-}\): conjugate base \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\)

A species that can act as both a Brönsted acid and a Brönsted base is amphiprotic: adding a proton gives its conjugate acid and removing one gives its conjugate base.

| Species | Conjugate acid | Conjugate base |
|---|---|---|
| \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) | \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\) | \(\text{OH}^-\) |
| \(\text{HCO}_3^-\) | \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\) | \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) |
| \(\text{HSO}_4^-\) | \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) | \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) |
| \(\text{NH}_3\) | \(\text{NH}_4^+\) | \(\text{NH}_2^-\) |

A Lewis acid accepts a lone pair of electrons; a Lewis base donates one.

(a) \(\text{OH}^-\) — Lewis BASE. The oxygen carries three lone pairs and can donate one, e.g. \(\text{H}^+ + {:}\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}\).

(b) \(\text{F}^-\) — Lewis BASE. It has four lone pairs and donates one, e.g. \(\text{BF}_3 + \text{F}^- \rightarrow \text{BF}_4^-\).

(c) \(\text{H}^+\) — Lewis ACID. Having an empty \(1s\) orbital it accepts a lone pair from a base such as \(\text{OH}^-\) or \(\text{NH}_3\).

(d) \(\text{BCl}_3\) — Lewis ACID. Boron has an incomplete octet (six electrons) and a vacant orbital, so it accepts a lone pair, e.g. \(\text{BCl}_3 + {:}\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{BCl}_3{:}\text{NH}_3\).

By the definition of pH, \(\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]\), so \([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}\).

\([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3.76}\)

\([\text{H}^+] = 1.74 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\)

For a conjugate acid-base pair, \(K_a \times K_b = K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\) at 298 K, so \(K_b = K_w/K_a\).

For \(\text{F}^-\) (conjugate base of \(\text{HF}\)):

\(K_b = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{6.8 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.47 \times 10^{-11}\)

For \(\text{HCOO}^-\) (conjugate base of \(\text{HCOOH}\)):

\(K_b = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{1.8 \times 10^{-4}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-11}\)

For \(\text{CN}^-\) (conjugate base of \(\text{HCN}\)):

\(K_b = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{4.8 \times 10^{-9}} = 2.08 \times 10^{-6}\)

The weakest acid \((\text{HCN})\) has the strongest conjugate base, as expected.

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- + \text{H}^+\), \(K_a = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\)

In pure \(0.05\,\text{M}\) phenol, let \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-] = x\). Since \(K_a\) is very small, \(0.05 - x \approx 0.05\):

\(K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{0.05}\), so \(x = \sqrt{(1.0 \times 10^{-10})(0.05)} = \sqrt{5 \times 10^{-12}}\)

\([\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-] = 2.24 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{M}\)

(Its degree of ionization here is \(\alpha = 2.24 \times 10^{-6}/0.05 = 4.47 \times 10^{-5}\).)

In the presence of \(0.01\,\text{M}\) sodium phenolate, the salt is fully dissociated and supplies the common ion, so \([\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-] \approx 0.01\,\text{M}\) and the ionization of phenol is suppressed:

\([\text{H}^+] = \dfrac{K_a[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}]}{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-]} = \dfrac{(1.0 \times 10^{-10})(0.05)}{0.01} = 5.0 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\)

Only this much phenol has ionized, so

\(\alpha = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{-10}}{0.05} = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\)

\(\text{H}_2\text{S} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HS}^-\), \(K_{a_1} = 9.1 \times 10^{-8}\); \(\text{HS}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{S}^{2-}\), \(K_{a_2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-13}\)

In \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) alone, the second step is negligible so \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{HS}^-] = x\):

\(x = \sqrt{K_{a_1} \times 0.1} = \sqrt{9.1 \times 10^{-9}}\), so \([\text{HS}^-] = 9.54 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

In a solution also \(0.1\,\text{M}\) in \(\text{HCl}\), the strong acid fixes \([\text{H}^+] \approx 0.1\,\text{M}\). By the common ion effect the first ionization is pushed back:

\([\text{HS}^-] = \dfrac{K_{a_1}[\text{H}_2\text{S}]}{[\text{H}^+]} = \dfrac{(9.1 \times 10^{-8})(0.1)}{0.1} = 9.1 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{M}\)

i.e. it falls by a factor of about \(10^3\).

For the sulphide ion, \([\text{S}^{2-}] = K_{a_2}[\text{HS}^-]/[\text{H}^+]\):

Without \(\text{HCl}\): \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{HS}^-]\), so \([\text{S}^{2-}] = K_{a_2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{M}\)

With \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\): \([\text{S}^{2-}] = \dfrac{(1.2 \times 10^{-13})(9.1 \times 10^{-8})}{0.1} = 1.09 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+\), \(K_a = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\), \(c = 0.05\,\text{M}\)

Using \(K_a = c\alpha^2/(1-\alpha)\) with \(\alpha \ll 1\), so \(K_a \approx c\alpha^2\) (Ostwald's dilution law):

\(\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{c}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.74 \times 10^{-5}}{0.05}} = \sqrt{3.48 \times 10^{-4}}\)

\(\alpha = 1.87 \times 10^{-2}\)

\([\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] = c\alpha = 0.05 \times 1.87 \times 10^{-2} = 9.33 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\)

Since \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]\),

\(\text{pH} = -\log(9.33 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.03\)

For the monobasic acid \(\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-\),

\([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-4.15} = 7.08 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Since each ionization gives one \(\text{H}^+\) and one anion,

\([\text{A}^-] = 7.08 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

The undissociated acid left is \([\text{HA}] = 0.01 - 7.08 \times 10^{-5} \approx 9.93 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\).

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} = \dfrac{(7.08 \times 10^{-5})^2}{9.93 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(K_a = 5.05 \times 10^{-7}\)

\(\text{p}K_a = -\log(5.05 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.30\)

Complete dissociation is assumed, so a strong monoacidic acid gives \([\text{H}^+]\) equal to its molarity and a strong monoacidic base gives \([\text{OH}^-]\) equal to its molarity; \(\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14\).

(a) \(0.003\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\): \([\text{H}^+] = 3 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\), \(\text{pH} = -\log(3 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.52\)

(b) \(0.005\,\text{M}\) \(\text{NaOH}\): \([\text{OH}^-] = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\), \(\text{pOH} = 2.30\), \(\text{pH} = 11.70\)

(c) \(0.002\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HBr}\): \([\text{H}^+] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\), \(\text{pH} = 2.70\)

(d) \(0.002\,\text{M}\) \(\text{KOH}\): \([\text{OH}^-] = 2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\), \(\text{pOH} = 2.70\), \(\text{pH} = 11.30\)

In each case find the molarity from mass / (molar mass x volume), then the ion concentration, then the pH. All four solutes are strong electrolytes.

a) \(\text{TlOH}\), molar mass \(= 204.4 + 16 + 1 = 221.4\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

\(n = 2/221.4 = 9.03 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\) in \(2\,\text{L}\), so \([\text{OH}^-] = 4.52 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = 2.35\), \(\text{pH} = 11.65\)

b) \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\), molar mass \(= 40 + 2(17) = 74\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); it gives two \(\text{OH}^-\) per formula unit.

\(n = 0.3/74 = 4.05 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\) in \(0.5\,\text{L}\), so \([\text{Ca(OH)}_2] = 8.11 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\) and \([\text{OH}^-] = 1.62 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = 1.79\), \(\text{pH} = 12.21\)

c) \(\text{NaOH}\), molar mass \(= 40\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

\(n = 0.3/40 = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\) in \(0.2\,\text{L}\), so \([\text{OH}^-] = 3.75 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = 1.43\), \(\text{pH} = 12.57\)

d) On dilution the moles are unchanged: \(n = 13.6 \times 1 \times 10^{-3} = 1.36 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\) in \(1\,\text{L}\), so \([\text{H}^+] = 1.36 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = 1.87\)

For a weak monobasic acid of concentration \(c\) and degree of ionization \(\alpha\),

\([\text{H}^+] = c\alpha = 0.1 \times 0.132 = 1.32 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log(1.32 \times 10^{-2}) = 1.88\)

Here \(\alpha\) is not small, so the full form of Ostwald's dilution law must be used:

\(K_a = \dfrac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha} = \dfrac{(0.1)(0.132)^2}{1-0.132} = \dfrac{1.742 \times 10^{-3}}{0.868}\)

\(K_a = 2.01 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(\text{p}K_a = -\log(2.01 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.70\)

Codeine is a weak base, \(\text{B} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{BH}^+ + \text{OH}^-\).

\(\text{pOH} = 14 - 9.95 = 4.05\), so \([\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-4.05} = 8.91 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Since \([\text{BH}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]\) and \([\text{B}] = 0.005 - 8.91 \times 10^{-5} = 4.91 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\),

\(K_b = \dfrac{[\text{BH}^+][\text{OH}^-]}{[\text{B}]} = \dfrac{(8.91 \times 10^{-5})^2}{4.91 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(K_b = 1.62 \times 10^{-6}\)

\(\text{p}K_b = -\log(1.62 \times 10^{-6}) = 5.79\)

From Table 6.7, \(K_b\) for aniline \(= 4.27 \times 10^{-10}\); \(c = 0.001\,\text{M}\).

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

Since \(K_b\) is very small, \(K_b \approx c\alpha^2\) and \([\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_b c}\):

\([\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{(4.27 \times 10^{-10})(0.001)} = \sqrt{4.27 \times 10^{-13}} = 6.53 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = -\log(6.53 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.19\), so \(\text{pH} = 7.81\)

Degree of ionization:

\(\alpha = \dfrac{[\text{OH}^-]}{c} = \dfrac{6.53 \times 10^{-7}}{0.001} = 6.53 \times 10^{-4}\)

For the conjugate acid (anilinium ion), \(K_a = K_w/K_b\):

\(K_a = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{4.27 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.34 \times 10^{-5}\)

\(K_a = 10^{-\text{p}K_a} = 10^{-4.74} = 1.82 \times 10^{-5}\)

In \(0.05\,\text{M}\) acetic acid alone, by Ostwald's dilution law,

\(\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{c}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.82 \times 10^{-5}}{0.05}} = 1.91 \times 10^{-2}\)

Adding \(\text{HCl}\) supplies the common ion \(\text{H}^+\), which by Le Chatelier's principle pushes the ionization back. Now \([\text{H}^+]\) is fixed by the strong acid and

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}]} = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+]\,c\alpha}{c(1-\alpha)} \approx [\text{H}^+]\alpha\), so \(\alpha \approx K_a/[\text{H}^+]\).

(a) In \(0.01\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\): \(\alpha = \dfrac{1.82 \times 10^{-5}}{0.01} = 1.82 \times 10^{-3}\)

(b) In \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\): \(\alpha = \dfrac{1.82 \times 10^{-5}}{0.1} = 1.82 \times 10^{-4}\)

So the degree of dissociation falls about tenfold and then a hundredfold below its value in pure water.

\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH}_2^+ + \text{OH}^-\), \(K_b = 5.4 \times 10^{-4}\), \(c = 0.02\,\text{M}\)

By Ostwald's dilution law \(K_b \approx c\alpha^2\):

\(\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_b}{c}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5.4 \times 10^{-4}}{0.02}} = \sqrt{0.027}\)

\(\alpha = 0.164\), i.e. about 16.4% ionized.

If the solution is also \(0.1\,\text{M}\) in \(\text{NaOH}\), the strong base fixes \([\text{OH}^-] \approx 0.1\,\text{M}\) and this common ion suppresses the ionization:

\(\alpha \approx \dfrac{K_b}{[\text{OH}^-]} = \dfrac{5.4 \times 10^{-4}}{0.1} = 5.4 \times 10^{-3}\)

So only \(0.54\%\) of the dimethylamine is ionized.

Using \([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}\):

Milk, \(\text{pH } 6.8\): \([\text{H}^+] = 1.58 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

Black coffee, \(\text{pH } 5.0\): \([\text{H}^+] = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Tomato juice, \(\text{pH } 4.2\): \([\text{H}^+] = 6.31 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Lemon juice, \(\text{pH } 2.2\): \([\text{H}^+] = 6.31 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\)

Egg white, \(\text{pH } 7.8\): \([\text{H}^+] = 1.58 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{M}\)

Egg white is the only one of the five that is basic \((\text{pH} > 7)\).

Molar mass of \(\text{KOH} = 39.1 + 16 + 1 = 56.1\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

\(n = 0.561/56.1 = 0.01\,\text{mol}\) in \(200\,\text{mL} = 0.2\,\text{L}\)

\([\text{KOH}] = 0.01/0.2 = 0.05\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{KOH}\) is a strong base and dissociates completely, so

\([\text{K}^+] = 0.05\,\text{M}\) and \([\text{OH}^-] = 0.05\,\text{M}\)

From \(K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-14}\),

\([\text{H}^+] = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{0.05} = 2 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log(2 \times 10^{-13}) = 12.70\)

Molar mass of \(\text{Sr(OH)}_2 = 87.6 + 2(17) = 121.6\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

Molar solubility \(= 19.23/121.6 = 0.1581\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(\text{Sr(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Sr}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-\), so each formula unit gives one \(\text{Sr}^{2+}\) and two \(\text{OH}^-\):

\([\text{Sr}^{2+}] = 0.1581\,\text{M}\)

\([\text{OH}^-] = 2 \times 0.1581 = 0.3163\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = -\log(0.3163) = 0.50\)

\(\text{pH} = 14 - 0.50 = 13.50\)

\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+\), \(K_a = 1.32 \times 10^{-5}\), \(c = 0.05\,\text{M}\)

By Ostwald's dilution law \(K_a \approx c\alpha^2\):

\(\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.32 \times 10^{-5}}{0.05}} = \sqrt{2.64 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.63 \times 10^{-2}\)

\([\text{H}^+] = c\alpha = 0.05 \times 1.63 \times 10^{-2} = 8.12 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log(8.12 \times 10^{-4}) = 3.09\)

If the solution is also \(0.01\,\text{M}\) in \(\text{HCl}\), the strong acid fixes \([\text{H}^+] \approx 0.01\,\text{M}\) and this common ion suppresses the ionization:

\(\alpha \approx \dfrac{K_a}{[\text{H}^+]} = \dfrac{1.32 \times 10^{-5}}{0.01} = 1.32 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(\text{HCNO} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{CNO}^-\)

\([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-2.34} = 4.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\), and \([\text{CNO}^-] = [\text{H}^+]\).

Undissociated acid: \([\text{HCNO}] = 0.1 - 4.57 \times 10^{-3} = 9.54 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{CNO}^-]}{[\text{HCNO}]} = \dfrac{(4.57 \times 10^{-3})^2}{9.54 \times 10^{-2}}\)

\(K_a = 2.19 \times 10^{-4}\)

Degree of ionization:

\(\alpha = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+]}{c} = \dfrac{4.57 \times 10^{-3}}{0.1} = 4.57 \times 10^{-2}\)

Sodium nitrite is the salt of a weak acid \((\text{HNO}_2)\) and a strong base, so the nitrite ion hydrolyses:

\(\text{NO}_2^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HNO}_2 + \text{OH}^-\)

For the conjugate pair, \(K_b = K_w/K_a\):

\(K_b = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{4.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 2.22 \times 10^{-11}\)

With \(c = 0.04\,\text{M}\) and \([\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_b c}\):

\([\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{(2.22 \times 10^{-11})(0.04)} = \sqrt{8.89 \times 10^{-13}} = 9.43 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = -\log(9.43 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.03\), so

\(\text{pH} = 7.97\)

Degree of hydrolysis:

\(h = \dfrac{[\text{OH}^-]}{c} = \dfrac{9.43 \times 10^{-7}}{0.04} = 2.36 \times 10^{-5}\)

Pyridinium hydrochloride is the salt of a weak base (pyridine) and a strong acid, so the pyridinium ion hydrolyses and the solution is acidic:

\(\text{C}_5\text{H}_5\text{NH}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_5\text{H}_5\text{N} + \text{H}^+\)

\([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3.44} = 3.63 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\)

Since \([\text{C}_5\text{H}_5\text{N}] = [\text{H}^+]\) and the salt concentration is essentially unchanged at \(0.02\,\text{M}\),

\(K_a(\text{pyridinium}) = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+]^2}{c} = \dfrac{(3.63 \times 10^{-4})^2}{0.02} = 6.59 \times 10^{-6}\)

For the conjugate pair, \(K_a \times K_b = K_w\):

\(K_b(\text{pyridine}) = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{6.59 \times 10^{-6}}\)

\(K_b = 1.52 \times 10^{-9}\)

A salt's solution is neutral if it comes from a strong acid and a strong base; basic if from a weak acid and a strong base (the anion hydrolyses); acidic if from a strong acid and a weak base (the cation hydrolyses).

\(\text{NaCl}\) — from \(\text{NaOH}\) (strong) and \(\text{HCl}\) (strong): NEUTRAL.

\(\text{KBr}\) — from \(\text{KOH}\) (strong) and \(\text{HBr}\) (strong): NEUTRAL.

\(\text{NaCN}\) — from \(\text{NaOH}\) (strong) and \(\text{HCN}\) (weak); \(\text{CN}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HCN} + \text{OH}^-\): BASIC.

\(\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3\) — from \(\text{NH}_4\text{OH}\) (weak) and \(\text{HNO}_3\) (strong); \(\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4\text{OH} + \text{H}^+\): ACIDIC.

\(\text{NaNO}_2\) — from \(\text{NaOH}\) (strong) and \(\text{HNO}_2\) (weak): BASIC.

\(\text{KF}\) — from \(\text{KOH}\) (strong) and \(\text{HF}\) (weak): BASIC.

For the acid, \(\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{ClCH}_2\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+\), \(K_a = 1.35 \times 10^{-3}\), \(c = 0.1\,\text{M}\). Here \(K_a\) is not small enough to neglect \(x\), so solve the quadratic:

\(\dfrac{x^2}{0.1-x} = 1.35 \times 10^{-3}\), i.e. \(x^2 + 1.35 \times 10^{-3}x - 1.35 \times 10^{-4} = 0\)

\(x = \dfrac{-1.35 \times 10^{-3} + \sqrt{(1.35 \times 10^{-3})^2 + 4(1.35 \times 10^{-4})}}{2} = 1.096 \times 10^{-2}\)

\(\text{pH (acid)} = -\log(1.096 \times 10^{-2}) = 1.96\)

For the sodium salt, the chloroacetate ion hydrolyses:

\(K_b = \dfrac{K_w}{K_a} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}{1.35 \times 10^{-3}} = 7.41 \times 10^{-12}\)

\([\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_b c} = \sqrt{(7.41 \times 10^{-12})(0.1)} = 8.61 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = 6.07\), so \(\text{pH (salt)} = 7.93\)

Water is neutral when \([\text{H}^+] = [\text{OH}^-]\), whatever the temperature. Then

\(K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = [\text{H}^+]^2\)

\([\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_w} = \sqrt{2.7 \times 10^{-14}} = 1.64 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log(1.64 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.78\)

So at 310 K neutral water has \(\text{pH } 6.78\), not 7 — the water is still neutral, because \(K_w\) itself has increased with temperature.

In each case count millimoles of \(\text{H}^+\) and \(\text{OH}^-\), find which is in excess, and divide by the TOTAL volume.

a) \(\text{OH}^- = 10 \times 0.2 \times 2 = 4.0\,\text{mmol}\); \(\text{H}^+ = 25 \times 0.1 = 2.5\,\text{mmol}\)

Excess \(\text{OH}^- = 1.5\,\text{mmol}\) in \(35\,\text{mL}\), so \([\text{OH}^-] = 4.29 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pOH} = 1.37\), \(\text{pH} = 12.63\)

b) \(\text{H}^+ = 10 \times 0.01 \times 2 = 0.2\,\text{mmol}\); \(\text{OH}^- = 10 \times 0.01 \times 2 = 0.2\,\text{mmol}\)

The acid and base exactly neutralise each other and the salt \(\text{CaSO}_4\) does not hydrolyse, so

\(\text{pH} = 7\)

c) \(\text{H}^+ = 10 \times 0.1 \times 2 = 2.0\,\text{mmol}\); \(\text{OH}^- = 10 \times 0.1 = 1.0\,\text{mmol}\)

Excess \(\text{H}^+ = 1.0\,\text{mmol}\) in \(20\,\text{mL}\), so \([\text{H}^+] = 0.05\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = 1.30\)

For a salt \(\text{M}_x\text{X}_y\) of molar solubility \(S\), \(K_{sp} = x^x y^y S^{(x+y)}\). Using the values of Table 6.9:

Silver chromate, \(\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4\), \(K_{sp} = 1.1 \times 10^{-12} = 4S^3\):

\(S = (2.75 \times 10^{-13})^{1/3} = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\); \([\text{Ag}^+] = 2S = 1.3 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\), \([\text{CrO}_4^{2-}] = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Barium chromate, \(\text{BaCrO}_4\), \(K_{sp} = 1.2 \times 10^{-10} = S^2\):

\(S = 1.1 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\); \([\text{Ba}^{2+}] = [\text{CrO}_4^{2-}] = 1.1 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Ferric hydroxide, \(\text{Fe(OH)}_3\), \(K_{sp} = 1.0 \times 10^{-38} = 27S^4\):

\(S = (3.70 \times 10^{-40})^{1/4} = 1.39 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\); \([\text{Fe}^{3+}] = 1.39 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\), \([\text{OH}^-] = 3S = 4.16 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\)

Lead chloride, \(\text{PbCl}_2\), \(K_{sp} = 1.6 \times 10^{-5} = 4S^3\):

\(S = (4.0 \times 10^{-6})^{1/3} = 1.59 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\); \([\text{Pb}^{2+}] = 1.59 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\), \([\text{Cl}^-] = 2S = 3.17 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\)

Mercurous iodide, \(\text{Hg}_2\text{I}_2\), which ionizes as \(\text{Hg}_2^{2+} + 2\text{I}^-\), \(K_{sp} = 4.5 \times 10^{-29} = 4S^3\):

\(S = (1.125 \times 10^{-29})^{1/3} = 2.24 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\); \([\text{Hg}_2^{2+}] = 2.24 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\), \([\text{I}^-] = 2S = 4.48 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{M}\)

(For \(\text{Fe(OH)}_3\) the calculated \([\text{OH}^-]\) is far below that supplied by water itself, so the figure is formal only.)

The relation between \(K_{sp}\) and solubility depends on the formula type, so the two must be treated separately.

For \(\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}^+ + \text{CrO}_4^{2-}\), \(K_{sp} = (2S_1)^2(S_1) = 4S_1^3\):

\(S_1 = \left(\dfrac{1.1 \times 10^{-12}}{4}\right)^{1/3} = (2.75 \times 10^{-13})^{1/3} = 6.50 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

For \(\text{AgBr} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ + \text{Br}^-\), \(K_{sp} = S_2^2\):

\(S_2 = \sqrt{5.0 \times 10^{-13}} = 7.07 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

\(\dfrac{S_1}{S_2} = \dfrac{6.50 \times 10^{-5}}{7.07 \times 10^{-7}} = 92.0\)

Silver chromate is about 92 times as soluble as silver bromide, even though its \(K_{sp}\) is larger by only a factor of about two — \(K_{sp}\) values may be compared directly only for salts of the same formula type.

On mixing equal volumes each concentration is halved:

\([\text{IO}_3^-] = 0.002/2 = 0.001\,\text{M}\) (from \(\text{NaIO}_3\))

\([\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 0.002/2 = 0.001\,\text{M}\) (from \(\text{Cu(ClO}_3)_2\))

For \(\text{Cu(IO}_3)_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{IO}_3^-\), the ionic product is

\(Q_{sp} = [\text{Cu}^{2+}][\text{IO}_3^-]^2 = (0.001)(0.001)^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-9}\)

Comparing with \(K_{sp} = 7.4 \times 10^{-8}\):

\(Q_{sp}\ (1.0 \times 10^{-9}) < K_{sp}\ (7.4 \times 10^{-8})\)

Since the ionic product is less than the solubility product, the solution is unsaturated and NO precipitation of copper iodate occurs.

In pure water, \(\text{AgC}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-\), so

\(S_0 = \sqrt{K_{sp}} = \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-13}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{M}\)

In an acidic buffer the benzoate ion is partly protonated, which removes it from solution and pulls more salt into solution. Only the fraction

\(f = \dfrac{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-]}{[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-] + [\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}]} = \dfrac{K_a}{K_a + [\text{H}^+]}\)

remains as free benzoate. At \(\text{pH } 3.19\), \([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-3.19} = 6.46 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\):

\(f = \dfrac{6.46 \times 10^{-5}}{6.46 \times 10^{-5} + 6.46 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.0910\)

If \(S\) is the new solubility, \([\text{Ag}^+] = S\) and \([\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-] = fS\), so

\(K_{sp} = fS^2\), giving \(S = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_{sp}}{f}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-13}}{0.0910}} = 1.66 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{M}\)

\(\dfrac{S}{S_0} = \dfrac{1.66 \times 10^{-6}}{5.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.3\)

Silver benzoate is about 3.3 times more soluble in the buffer of \(\text{pH } 3.19\) than in pure water.

It prints \(2.5 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{M}\), which is exactly \(\sqrt{K_{sp}} = 2.510 \times 10^{-9}\), i.e. the ion concentration AFTER the two solutions are mixed. The question asks for the concentration of the solutions that are then mixed in equal volumes, and mixing equal volumes halves each concentration, so the solutions may be twice as concentrated: \(5.02 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{M}\). Both values are named here because a reader who takes "the solution" to mean the mixture will arrive at the key's figure, and because an examiner following the book will expect it.] Let the concentration of each solution before mixing be \(c\). Mixing equal volumes halves each:

\([\text{Fe}^{2+}] = [\text{S}^{2-}] = c/2\)

Precipitation is just avoided when the ionic product equals the solubility product:

\(Q_{sp} = [\text{Fe}^{2+}][\text{S}^{2-}] = (c/2)^2 \leq K_{sp} = 6.3 \times 10^{-18}\)

\(c/2 \leq \sqrt{6.3 \times 10^{-18}} = 2.51 \times 10^{-9}\)

\(c \leq 5.02 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{M}\)

So the maximum concentration of each solution is \(5.02 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

For \(\text{CaSO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\), \(K_{sp} = S^2\):

\(S = \sqrt{9.1 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.02 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Molar mass of \(\text{CaSO}_4 = 40 + 32 + 4(16) = 136\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so the solubility in grams per litre is

\(3.02 \times 10^{-3} \times 136 = 0.410\,\text{g L}^{-1}\)

A saturated solution therefore holds \(0.410\,\text{g}\) in \(1\,\text{L}\), so the minimum volume needed to dissolve \(1\,\text{g}\) is

\(V = \dfrac{1}{0.410} = 2.44\,\text{L}\)
